[BAYDAWI-FULL:39:24-26/r3] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The overt description wrongdoers replaces a pronoun to register their wrongdoing and identify why they are addressed this way.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:39:24-26/r4] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | They are told to taste the consequence of what they earned; the waw is circumstantial with an implicit qad.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p53/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The omitted comparison asks whether someone shielding himself with his face is like one safe from punishment.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p53/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The phrase means the severity of punishment.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p53/r3] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | People shield their precious face with a hand; one thrown into Hell has hands bound to the neck and can shield himself only with his face.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p53/r4] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The speakers are the keepers of Hell, addressing wrongdoers.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p53/r5] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | What they are told to taste is the recompense of what they earned.
[QASHANI:39:22-24/r9] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | The punished person has the face, the noblest organ, exposed because bodily dispositions bind the other limbs and prevent movement to protect himself, unlike one secure from punishment.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p196#2/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الشاعر | reports | The poem depicts a warrior meeting swords with his face and neck, illustrating boldness in facing a blow without a shield.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p196#2/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari supplies the omitted comparison as one safe from punishment; Ibn Atiyya instead compares him to the blessed in Paradise.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p196#2/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The keepers of Hell address the wrongdoers: taste the consequences of the evil deeds you used to commit.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p196/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عطية | prefers | Ibn Atiyya prefers the eloquent sense of progressively worsening punishment: the victim first guards himself with limbs, then ultimately with his honored face.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p196/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Ittaqā can mean to receive or meet something, as in the cited poem where a woman raises a hand to shield herself from view.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p196/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid says the condemned person is dragged on his face through the Fire.
[SAMIN-DURR:39:22/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari supplies the comparison with one safe from punishment. | mentions 39:24
[SAMIN-DURR:39:22/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن عطية | reports | Ibn Atiyya supplies the comparison with those blessed in Paradise. | mentions 39:24
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p65#3/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | The two hadiths describe the Quran's companion as being in a blessed, enviable state; one should wish for the same blessing and congratulate him.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p65#3/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Ghibta means wishing for another's blessing without its removal; condemned envy wishes the blessing removed, whether or not the envier gets it, and was Iblis's first sin against Adam.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p65#3/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | The praiseworthy form of hasad is wishing for the same good state, not its loss to someone else.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p65#3/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet's statement that there is no hasad except in two cases refers to the Quran reader's private blessing and the charitable spender's benefit to others; Ibn Kathir links it to 35:29. | mentions 35:29
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p65#3/r5] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Yazid ibn al-Akhnas reports the Prophet saying that competition should be limited to a person devoted to the Quran and a person who gives away wealth in charity.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p65#3/r6] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · أبو كبشة | reports | Abu Kabsha reports the Prophet dividing people into four: learned and charitable wealth is best; knowledge without wealth earns equal reward when the person intends good; ignorant wealth is squandered; and the poor ignorant person's corrupt wish carries equal burden.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p95#2/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | The condemned is reproached with the punishment earned, unlike the person who comes safely on Judgment Day; Ibn Kathīr compares this with face-walking and fire references. | mentions 67:22, 54:48, 41:40
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p95#2/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | The verse states only one side of the comparison; the poet's line about seeking good leaves its opposite unstated, meaning good or evil. | mentions 67:22, 54:48, 41:40
[BURHAN:v2p344/r7] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | A literal comparison question requires an omitted counterpart: here the comparison is with someone enjoying Paradise.
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p440/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | After contrasting the expanded and constricted breast and concluding that one is guided and the other astray, the passage unfolds each group’s outcome in a deliberately interwoven interrogative; misguidance leads to punishment and guidance to bliss.
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p440/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The singular follows the form من so the wording does not suggest that the faces are those of leaders; the face becomes a shield because the hand, normally used to ward off danger, is bound, and the honored face must protect the rest of the body.
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p440/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The wrongdoer is thrown upside down into Hell, bound, with no free limb to shield his face; a mountain-like sulfur stone hangs at his neck and he is dragged face-first, unlike the one who receives bliss in heart and body.
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p440/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The passive وقيل fits the general character of reproach; the text could have said “to him,” but instead names the wrongdoers and uses the plural to generalize the judgment and show their numbers do not help them.
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p440/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The wrongdoers are those who abandoned guidance, followed desire, and went astray while leading others astray.
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p440/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | They are told to taste the recompense of what they used to regard as the benefit and fruit of their deeds and conduct.
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p440/r7] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | By ellipsis through correspondence, the opening question implies the omitted counterpart, and the words addressed to wrongdoers imply that the righteous are told to be content and take delight as recompense for their deeds.
[DURR-FULL:v7p222/r6] DURR-FULL, d. 911 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid says the condemned person is dragged on his face through the Fire, comparing this to the question in 41:40 about who is safer on the Day of Resurrection. | mentions 41:40
[DURR-FULL:v7p222/r7] DURR-FULL, d. 911 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says the condemned person is taken bound to Hell and thrown in, so that his face is the first part touched by the Fire.
[ITQAN:v2p580#2/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | Conjunction may attach to wording, syntactic position, or imagined construction; positional conjunction requires a licit, original position and a live trigger.
[ITQAN:v2p580#2/r2] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | Positional-conjunction conditions exclude forms such as “I passed by Zayd and Amr,” a governed adjective plus genitive, and coordination after إن removes the original subject trigger.
[ITQAN:v2p580#2/r5] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | Conjunction by imagined construction requires that the imagined particle could actually occur; it is strongest when common, as in a genitive phrase and Zuhayr’s line.

[BURSEVI:v8p75#2/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The hamza is interrogative denial, the fa connects to an omitted proposition, and the conditional has an omitted predicate: are people equal, when the unbeliever must shield himself with his face, his noblest limb?
[BURSEVI:v8p75#2/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | اتقى بكذا means making something a shield against what harms oneself; here the unbeliever uses his face as a shield.
[BURSEVI:v8p75#3/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · الكاشفي | reports | Al-Kashifi's Persian commentary glosses the evil punishment as the flame of fire.
[BURSEVI:v8p75#3/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | On Judgment Day the unbeliever's hands are shackled to his neck, unlike the safe believer, so he must ward off punishment with his face.
[BURSEVI:v8p75#3/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · التأويلات النجمية | reports | Al-Ta'wilat al-Najmiyya reads it as turning one's face toward the evil punishment to fend it off, unlike one who does not protect himself and wrongs himself.
[BURSEVI:v8p75#3/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The wrongdoers are those who substituted disbelief for faith, denial for affirmation, and disobedience for obedience; the command is spoken by the keepers of Hell.
[BURSEVI:v8p75#3/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The past-tense wording signals certainty; naming them explicitly as wrongdoers records their guilt and explains the order to taste punishment.
[BURSEVI:v8p76/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Their recompense is what they continually earned in worldly life through disbelief, denial, and sins.
[BURSEVI:v8p76/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · التأويلات النجمية | reports | Al-Ta'wilat al-Najmiyya says they had been within punishment through vile acts and traits but did not taste it while asleep in heedlessness; death awakened them to it.
[ALUSI-FULL:v23p260#2/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The verse resumes the argument to explain the contrast between the guided and the astray.
[ALUSI-FULL:v23p260#2/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | “It was said to the wrongdoers” may coordinate with “protects himself”; the past tense signals certainty. Alternatively, it is a circumstantial clause, with or without an implied “already.”
[ALUSI-FULL:v23p260#2/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The explicit noun “wrongdoers” replaces a pronoun to condemn them and signal why they are told to taste punishment.
[ALUSI-FULL:v23p260#2/r12] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | They are commanded to taste the continuing consequence of their worldly earnings in disbelief and sins.
[ALUSI-FULL:v23p260#2/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The omitted premise is “are all people equal?”: is the person forced to ward off punishment with his face like one safe from harm and in no need of protection?
[ALUSI-FULL:v23p260#2/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The face is literal: his hand, which once warded off harms, is chained to his neck, leaving him to shield himself with his most honored limb.
[ALUSI-FULL:v23p260#2/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Even without the report that the hand is chained, taking the face literally vividly depicts the completeness and earnestness of his self-protection.
[ALUSI-FULL:v23p260#2/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | The face may mean the whole person, making the image hyperbolic.
[ALUSI-FULL:v23p260#2/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | Another view treats face-protection as a figure for having no shield at all, since the face is not a means of protection; Alusi finds this strained.
[ALUSI-FULL:v23p260#2/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | “On the Day of Resurrection” may be governed by “protects himself,” or attached to “the evil of punishment,” meaning the punishment of that Day; Alusi calls the latter sound but the former more immediate.
[ALUSI-FULL:v23p260#2/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The cited line depicts the literal face and chest meeting swords, with the head serving as a helmet.
[ALUSI-FULL:v23p260#2/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Alusi says the verse was revealed about Abu Jahl.
[ELMALILI:39:22-31/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | He pictures the wrongdoer as using his face to shield himself from the evil punishment on Judgment Day.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p48/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The third kind of revelation occasion is a recurring sort of event involving one person; the verse announces its rule and rebukes whoever commits it.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p48/r10] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Many disagreements among Companions over occasions of revelation illustrate this fourth kind; al-Suyuti discusses it with examples in the fifth issue of his al-Itqan treatment.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p48/r11] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas reports that a man with a small flock greeted pursuing Muslims with salam, was killed as a supposed unbeliever, and had his flock taken; the verse then came down. | mentions 4:94
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p48/r12] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The story must have happened, since Ibn Abbas transmitted it, but the verse was not revealed exclusively for it; its context places it among rules of jihad. | mentions 4:94
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p48/r13] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · الزبير | reports | After his water dispute with an Ansari at the streams of al-Harra, al-Zubayr said he thought the verses about submitting disputes to the Prophet had been revealed about that event. | mentions 4:65
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p48/r14] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · الزركشي | reports | Al-Zarkashi says a Companion or Successor who says “revealed about this” commonly means the verse includes that ruling, not that this event caused its revelation.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p48/r15] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · ابن تيمية | reports | Ibn Taymiyya records disagreement over whether a Companion’s “revealed about this” is a transmitted report or exegesis: al-Bukhari counts it as musnad, while most hadith compilers do not.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p48/r16] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · ابن تيمية | reports | Ibn Taymiyya distinguishes a general “revealed about this” statement from an account naming an event immediately preceding revelation, which all compilers treat as musnad.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p48/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Exegetes saying a verse was revealed about an event may mean that the event is one example covered by the verse, not its exclusive occasion.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p48/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · عبد الله بن مسعود | reports | Ibn Masud reports the Prophet’s warning that one who swears falsely to seize a Muslim’s property will meet God angry; revelation confirmed this warning. | mentions 3:77
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p48/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · الأشعث بن قيس | reports | Ashath ibn Qays said the verse about the false oath was revealed concerning him and a well on his cousin’s land. | mentions 3:77
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p48/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Ibn Masud treated the verse as general confirmation of a general prophetic report, whereas Ashath took his own “it was revealed about me” as exclusive. | mentions 3:77
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p48/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas said they called the opening passages about hypocrites in Surat al-Tawba “the exposer.”
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p48/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The verse about disbelievers not wanting good to descend is another case where no special occasion needs to be supplied merely because some Jews showed Muslims affection. | mentions 2:105
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p48/r8] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Storytellers and some exegetes overemphasize this kind of occasion without benefit; it can mislead less informed readers into restricting a verse whose wording does not visibly state its generality.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p48/r9] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The fourth kind is an event whose circumstances fit the meaning of surrounding Qur’anic passages, so early Muslims may seem to identify it as the specific occasion when they mean it falls under the verse.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v23p391/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The verse interrupts Qur’an-praise before 39:27; commentators connect it to the two outcomes in 39:23, with an omitted comparison and a reportive or rejecting question: the punished and the blessed are not equal. | mentions 39:23, 39:27
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v23p391/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The omitted comparison is with one safe from punishment through God’s guidance, as in the parallel question at 47:14; the guided do not suffer the torment. | mentions 39:19, 39:22, 47:14
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v23p393/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | prefers | Ibn ʿAshur’s preferred construction makes the question identify the referent of “whoever God leads astray” in 39:23: the omitted subject is “is he the one who shields his face from torment?” | mentions 39:23
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v23p393/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Ittiqāʾ means undertaking protection, restraint, and warding off; waqā takes two objects and may mark the instrument of protection with bi.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v23p393/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · النابغة | reports | Al-Nābigha’s verse, “she protected us with her hand,” illustrates bi marking the means by which protection is achieved.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v23p393/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | With the iftiʿāl form, the verb takes one object, which was the second object of the base verb waqā.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v23p393/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Since the face is most precious and normally shielded from blows, claiming to shield oneself with one’s face is sarcastic allusion to having no protection; compare 18:29. | mentions 18:29
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v23p393/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | “The evil of the torment” is the object of ittqā; in the base construction it is the second object of waqā, but the derived

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v23p393/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | “And it was said” may be coordinated with the relative clause, with “whoever” understood collectively as “they”; “the wrongdoers” replaces a pronoun to imply their punishment is caused by their shirk.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v23p393/r8] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The one with no shield against punishment is told to taste the torment.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v23p393/r9] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Alternatively, “the wrongdoers” broadly includes polytheists from all peoples; the sentence then sums up their common fate and leads into the denial by earlier peoples in 39:25. | mentions 39:25
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v23p394/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The past form depicts a certain future as already past; alternatively, the clause is circumstantial with an implicit قد, so the tense needs no such reinterpretation.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v23p394/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Taste is a metaphor for bodily sensation: the tongue's sense is stronger than the skin's, and the comparison rests on intensity.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v23p394/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The tasted punishment repays their worldly acquisition of shirk and its practices; equating punishment with their deeds stresses just recompense corresponding to their actions.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v23p394/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The wording تكسبون instead of تعملون attributes the punishment to what they acquired, cutting off the protest of people who resent their torment.
[TABATABAI:39:23-29/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The verse contrasts the people of punishment with those secure from it, representing the misguided and the guided and continuing the previous verse. | mentions 39:23
[TABATABAI:39:23-29/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The interrogative is rejecting; the predicate after “whoever” is omitted, understood as “like one who is safe from it.”
[TABATABAI:39:23-29/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī construes “on the Day of Resurrection” as modifying “guards himself.”
[TABATABAI:39:23-29/r6] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · قيل | reports | One view says the person shields himself with his face because his hand, normally used to ward off harm, is shackled to his neck.
[TABATABAI:39:23-29/r7] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | rejects | Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī objects that the face is not a means of shielding oneself; an alternative reading makes the phrase refer to warding off future punishment through piety, but he finds it forced.
[TABATABAI:39:23-29/r8] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The speakers telling the wrongdoers to taste the result of their deeds are the angels of the Fire; the clause may include an implied qad or not.
[TABATABAI:39:23-29/r9] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Calling them “the wrongdoers” instead of using a pronoun identifies their wrongdoing as the cause of the sentence.
[ASAD-NOTES:39:24#n31/r1] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | Protecting oneself with one's face is an idiom meaning that the person has nothing whatever with which to shield himself.
[BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p602/r1] BINTSHATI-IJAZ, d. 1419 · author | holds | Some Arabic scholars were wary of interpreting Qur'anic ambiguities, rare words, and alleged antonyms.
[BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p602/r3] BINTSHATI-IJAZ, d. 1419 · أبو حاتم السجستاني | holds | The Basran linguist and Qur'an scholar Abu Hatim was strongly cautious about interpreting Qur'anic antonyms and criticized those who ventured beyond their Arabic knowledge.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p546/r10] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | God will show no mercy at the helplessness of wrongdoers when they face punishment.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p546/r6] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | The enunciative khabar is suppressed in the interrogative sentence, and Islahi supplies it in his translation.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p546/r7] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | The punishment will be so terrible that the arrogant will try to use their faces as shields, with no other protection available.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p546/r8] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | The face is a person’s most valued and protected part, making its use as a shield an especially stark reversal.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p546/r9] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | The wrongdoers are the arrogant people who rejected the Qur’an and thereby wronged themselves.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:39:24/r1] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | reports | Commentators see a comparison between two kinds of people: the condemned disbeliever is mentioned, while the implied counterpart is the believer who needs no afterlife protection from fire, deserves happiness, or is in Paradise; these descriptions convey substantially the same idea (Tabari; Shawkani).
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:39:24/r2] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | reports | Ibn Ashur explains that using one’s face to shield oneself from severe punishment expresses the condemned person’s utter helplessness: even the most valuable part of the body cannot be protected.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:39:24/r3] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | The wrongdoers are those who commit the greatest injustice by assigning divinity to another or denying God, along with other wrongs; their own deeds and acquisitions bring this fate.
[QIRAAT-ER:39:24:11#1/r1] QIRAAT-ER · author | holds | Vowel harmony gives qīla a rounded transitional vowel after wāw while retaining the passive q-w-l form.
[STUDYQURAN:39:24/r1] STUDYQURAN · IK, Ṭ | reports | An omitted comparison asks whether this person is like one who does right; parallel contrasts appear in 41:40 and 67:22. | mentions 41:40, 67:22
[STUDYQURAN:39:24/r2] STUDYQURAN · Q, Ṭ | reports | Guarding with his face may mean that the face is the first part to touch the Fire.
[STUDYQURAN:39:24/r3] STUDYQURAN · Q, Ṭ | reports | Alternatively, the phrase may describe someone dragged into the Fire on his face.
[STUDYQURAN:39:24/r4] STUDYQURAN · author | holds | Taste that which you used to earn echoes the punishment statement in 7:39. | mentions 7:39
